message.content:
Before the middle of the fifteenth century, the written word in Europe was a rare and precious commodity. Books were copied by hand, usually by monks in monastic scriptoria, a laborious process that could take months or even years for a single volume. A well-produced manuscript might cost as much as a house, and the total number of books in all of Christendom before 1450 is estimated at no more than a few hundred thousand. Literacy, correspondingly, was confined to a narrow stratum of society: the clergy, a small professional class of lawyers and administrators, and a thin layer of wealthy laypeople who could afford to maintain private tutors. The vast majority of Europeans lived their entire lives without ever reading a book.
